guided.title: Build the customer table
guided.prompt: The DataFrame `flat` repeats each customer on every order line. Build `customers` with the columns `email` and `name`, one row per email (keep the first row for each email), with the index reset. Print `customers.to_string(index=False)`. Expected output: three lines, a header and the rows for ana@x.com and ben@x.com.
guided.starter:
import pandas as pd

flat = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [1, 1, 2, 3],
    "email": ["ana@x.com", "ana@x.com", "ben@x.com", "ana@x.com"],
    "name": ["Ana", "Ana", "Ben", "Ana"],
    "qty": [2, 1, 4, 5],
})
customers = flat
print(customers.to_string(index=False))
guided.solution:
import pandas as pd

flat = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [1, 1, 2, 3],
    "email": ["ana@x.com", "ana@x.com", "ben@x.com", "ana@x.com"],
    "name": ["Ana", "Ana", "Ben", "Ana"],
    "qty": [2, 1, 4, 5],
})
customers = flat[["email", "name"]].drop_duplicates(subset="email").reset_index(drop=True)
print(customers.to_string(index=False))
guided.expected:
email name
ana@x.com  Ana
ben@x.com  Ben
hints: Select the two columns first with a list of names.
`drop_duplicates` takes `subset=` to decide which columns define a duplicate.

guided.title: Add surrogate keys
guided.prompt: Starting from the `customers` table below, add a column `customer_key` with the integers 1, 2, ... in row order, then merge it into `flat` on `email` (left join, `validate="m:1"`) and print the list of `customer_key` values of `flat` in its row order. Expected output: `[1, 1, 2, 1]`.
guided.starter:
import pandas as pd

flat = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [1, 1, 2, 3],
    "email": ["ana@x.com", "ana@x.com", "ben@x.com", "ana@x.com"],
    "name": ["Ana", "Ana", "Ben", "Ana"],
    "qty": [2, 1, 4, 5],
})
customers = flat[["email", "name"]].drop_duplicates(subset="email").reset_index(drop=True)
print(flat["qty"].tolist())
guided.solution:
import pandas as pd

flat = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [1, 1, 2, 3],
    "email": ["ana@x.com", "ana@x.com", "ben@x.com", "ana@x.com"],
    "name": ["Ana", "Ana", "Ben", "Ana"],
    "qty": [2, 1, 4, 5],
})
customers = flat[["email", "name"]].drop_duplicates(subset="email").reset_index(drop=True)
customers["customer_key"] = customers.index + 1
merged = flat.merge(customers[["email", "customer_key"]], on="email", how="left", validate="m:1")
print(merged["customer_key"].tolist())
hints: Add 1 to the index to start the keys at 1.

guided.title: Find conflicting keys
guided.prompt: The rows below describe products. Print the list of `code` values that have more than one distinct `title`, sorted. Expected output: `['P2']`.
guided.starter:
import pandas as pd

rows = pd.DataFrame({"code": ["P1", "P2", "P2", "P3", "P1"], "title": ["Pen", "Book", "Notebook", "Ink", "Pen"]})
print([])
guided.solution:
import pandas as pd

rows = pd.DataFrame({"code": ["P1", "P2", "P2", "P3", "P1"], "title": ["Pen", "Book", "Notebook", "Ink", "Pen"]})
counts = rows.groupby("code")["title"].nunique()
print(sorted(counts[counts > 1].index.tolist()))
hints: Count the distinct titles for each code.
Keep the entries above 1 and print their index as a sorted list.

guided.title: List the orphans
guided.prompt: `orders` refers to customers by `customer_id`; `customers` lists the existing ids. Print the sorted list of distinct `customer_id` values in `orders` that are missing from `customers`. Expected output: `[7, 9]`.
guided.starter:
import pandas as pd

customers = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2, 3]})
orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [10, 11, 12, 13], "customer_id": [1, 7, 3, 9]})
print([])
guided.solution:
import pandas as pd

customers = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2, 3]})
orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [10, 11, 12, 13], "customer_id": [1, 7, 3, 9]})
missing = orders[~orders["customer_id"].isin(customers["customer_id"])]
print(sorted(missing["customer_id"].unique().tolist()))
hints: Negate the mask with `~` to get the rows that are not found.
Take the unique `customer_id` values of the unmatched rows and sort them.

independent.title: Split and prove it
independent.prompt: Split `flat` into `customers` (`customer_key`, `email`, `name`), `products` (`product_key`, `code`, `title`) and `lines` (`order_id`, `customer_key`, `product_key`, `qty`), with surrogate keys numbered from 1 in order of first appearance. Print on the first line the three row counts separated by spaces (`customers products lines`), on the second line `True` or `False` for whether joining the three tables back, selecting `order_id, email, name, code, title, qty`, sorting by `order_id` and `code` and resetting the index equals `flat` sorted the same way, and on the third line whether every key column is unique in its table (`True`/`False`). Expected output: `2 2 5`, `True`, `True`.
independent.starter:
import pandas as pd

flat = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [1, 1, 2, 3, 3],
    "email": ["ana@x.com", "ana@x.com", "ben@x.com", "ana@x.com", "ana@x.com"],
    "name": ["Ana", "Ana", "Ben", "Ana", "Ana"],
    "code": ["P1", "P2", "P1", "P1", "P2"],
    "title": ["Pen", "Book", "Pen", "Pen", "Book"],
    "qty": [2, 1, 4, 1, 3],
})
# split, join back, compare
independent.solution:
import pandas as pd

flat = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [1, 1, 2, 3, 3],
    "email": ["ana@x.com", "ana@x.com", "ben@x.com", "ana@x.com", "ana@x.com"],
    "name": ["Ana", "Ana", "Ben", "Ana", "Ana"],
    "code": ["P1", "P2", "P1", "P1", "P2"],
    "title": ["Pen", "Book", "Pen", "Pen", "Book"],
    "qty": [2, 1, 4, 1, 3],
})
customers = flat[["email", "name"]].drop_duplicates(subset="email").reset_index(drop=True)
customers.insert(0, "customer_key", customers.index + 1)
products = flat[["code", "title"]].drop_duplicates(subset="code").reset_index(drop=True)
products.insert(0, "product_key", products.index + 1)
lines = (flat[["order_id", "email", "code", "qty"]]
         .merge(customers[["email", "customer_key"]], on="email", validate="m:1")
         .merge(products[["code", "product_key"]], on="code", validate="m:1")
         [["order_id", "customer_key", "product_key", "qty"]])
print(len(customers), len(products), len(lines))
back = (lines.merge(customers, on="customer_key").merge(products, on="product_key")
        [["order_id", "email", "name", "code", "title", "qty"]]
        .sort_values(["order_id", "code"]).reset_index(drop=True))
want = flat.sort_values(["order_id", "code"]).reset_index(drop=True)
print(back.equals(want))
print(customers["customer_key"].is_unique and products["product_key"].is_unique and customers["email"].is_unique)

independent.title: Relationship report for sheets
independent.prompt: `book` imitates `read_excel(sheet_name=None)` for a workbook with sheets `Customers` and `Orders`. Print three lines: `duplicate customer ids: ` and the sorted list of customer ids that appear more than once in `Customers`; `empty customer ids in orders: ` and how many rows of `Orders` have a missing `customer_id`; `orphan orders: ` and the sorted list of `order_id` values whose non-missing `customer_id` is not in `Customers`. Expected output: `duplicate customer ids: [2]`, `empty customer ids in orders: 1`, `orphan orders: [12, 14]`.
independent.starter:
import pandas as pd

nan = float("nan")
book = {
    "Customers": pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2, 2, 3], "name": ["Ana", "Ben", "Ben B.", "Cy"]}),
    "Orders": pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [10, 11, 12, 13, 14], "customer_id": [1, nan, 8, 3, 9]}),
}
# report
independent.solution:
import pandas as pd

nan = float("nan")
book = {
    "Customers": pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 2, 2, 3], "name": ["Ana", "Ben", "Ben B.", "Cy"]}),
    "Orders": pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [10, 11, 12, 13, 14], "customer_id": [1, nan, 8, 3, 9]}),
}
customers, orders = book["Customers"], book["Orders"]
dup = customers.loc[customers["customer_id"].duplicated(keep=False), "customer_id"].unique().tolist()
print("duplicate customer ids:", sorted(dup))
print("empty customer ids in orders:", int(orders["customer_id"].isna().sum()))
known = orders[orders["customer_id"].notna()]
orphans = known[~known["customer_id"].isin(customers["customer_id"])]
print("orphan orders:", sorted(orphans["order_id"].tolist()))
independent.expected:
duplicate customer ids: [2]
empty customer ids in orders: 1
orphan orders: [12, 14]

independent.title: Design the split for your own sheet
independent.prompt: Pick a flat spreadsheet you know (invoices, timesheets, a shop export). Name its grain, the entity tables you would split out, each table's key (natural or surrogate, and why), the relationships, and the three checks you would run before loading.
independent.solution: For a timesheet export where every row is one person on one project on one day: the grain is person-project-day. Entities: `employee` (key `employee_id`, natural, issued by HR), `project` (key `project_code`, natural, stable), and `time_entry` (key `employee_id, project_code, work_date`, composite). Relationships: one employee has many time entries and one project has many time entries, both through foreign keys in `time_entry`. Checks before loading: every key column is unique in its parent table, no `time_entry` row has an orphan `employee_id` or `project_code`, and the join of the three tables reproduces the original row count and the sum of hours.
rubric: Names the grain of the sheet
Separates at least two entities with keys and explains the key choice
States the one-to-many relationships and where the foreign key lives
Lists uniqueness, orphan and join-back checks

checks.question: What does `df.drop_duplicates()` (no arguments) do on a sheet where one customer appears on two rows that differ only in the city?
options: Keeps one row for the customer
Keeps both rows, because they are not identical in every column
Raises an error because of the conflict
Keeps the row with the longer city
checks.explanation: Without `subset`, pandas compares all columns, so rows that differ in any column are different. Deduplicate on the key and check for disagreement with `nunique()`.

checks.question: What does `validate="m:1"` in `merge` do?
options: Sorts the result by key
Raises an error if the right-hand table has a repeated key
Removes unmatched rows
Converts the key to integers
checks.explanation: The check says many rows on the left match at most one on the right. If the lookup repeats a key, the merge would multiply rows, so pandas raises `MergeError` instead.

checks.question: `orders` has `customer_id` values 1, 2, 7 and `customers` has 1, 2, 3. Which statement is true after an inner join on `customer_id`?
options: All three orders are kept
The order of customer 7 disappears without any error
pandas raises because 7 is missing
Customer 3 is added with empty order columns
checks.explanation: An inner join keeps only matching keys, so the orphan row is dropped silently. That is why you list orphans first. A left join would keep the order with empty customer columns; an outer join would also add customer 3.

checks.question: Why do many pipelines add a surrogate key even when an email address is available?
options: Emails cannot be stored in databases
A natural key can change or be reused, while an invented integer stays stable and keeps foreign keys small
Surrogate keys make queries slower but safer
Pandas requires integers for merges
checks.explanation: If a person changes their email, every foreign key that stored the email would need rewriting. A surrogate key stays the same and the email becomes an ordinary unique column.

checks.question: What proves that splitting a flat sheet lost nothing?
options: The new tables have fewer rows
Joining the new tables back reproduces the original rows (sorted comparison)
`drop_duplicates` ran without error
Every table has a primary key
checks.explanation: Only a comparison with the original shows that no row or value was lost or duplicated. Fewer rows are expected in the lookup tables and says nothing about correctness.

environment.note: Example 1 writes a three-sheet workbook with openpyxl into a temporary folder and reads it back with `pd.read_excel(path, sheet_name=None)`; the browser cannot import openpyxl, so run it locally after `pip install openpyxl pandas`. The other examples and every graded exercise express the same workbook as DataFrames, and `sqlite3` stands in for PostgreSQL (type names and some syntax differ, but primary keys, foreign key columns and joins behave as taught).
